passages.t: Three days at the river, and the ark goes first
passages.happening:
Early in the morning Joshua moves the whole camp from Shittim down to the edge of the Jordan. They wait there three days (verses 1-2).

Then the officers go through the camp with instructions. “When you see the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God being carried by the Levitical priests, you are to set out from your positions and follow it” (verse 3). The people are to keep well back from it, about two thousand cubits, ‘so that you can see the way to go, since you have never traveled this way before’ (verse 4).

Joshua tells the people, “Consecrate yourselves, for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you” (verse 5). And he tells the priests to take up the ark and go ahead (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
For three days Israel camped beside a river it could not cross. It was spring, and the Jordan was in flood. The people had time to look at the water and to understand that no plan of their own would get a whole nation, with children, old people and herds, to the other side.

The ark of the covenant was a wooden chest covered with gold. Inside were the stone tablets of the covenant made at Sinai. Its lid had two winged figures on it, and Israel thought of it as the throne or the footstool of the God no one could see. It was the sign that God was present with his people. Priests carried it on poles, and no one else was to touch it.

In the wilderness the people had followed a pillar of cloud. Now they are told to follow the ark. God is not sending Israel into the river. He is going in first.

Two thousand cubits is about half a mile. The distance did two things. It showed respect for the holiness of God. It also meant that the whole people, spread out behind, could see the ark and know which way to walk. A crowd pressed close around it would have hidden it from everyone but the front row.

To consecrate themselves meant to get ready to meet God. At Mount Sinai that had included washing their clothes. The crossing is being prepared like an act of worship and not like a military move.

The line ‘you have never traveled this way before’ is simple and true. Nothing in forty years of desert had prepared them for this, and the instruction is plain: keep your eyes on the ark.
passages.later:
At the Red Sea, forty years before, the same God had made a way where there was none: “and the Israelites went through the sea on dry ground, with walls of water on their right and on their left” (Exodus 14:22).

A later prophet heard God make a promise that sounds like this morning at the Jordan: “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and when you go through the rivers, they will not overwhelm you” (Isaiah 43:2).
passages.asks: Israel waited three days beside a river it could not cross, and then was told only to watch the ark and follow. Ask what stands in front of you that you ‘have never traveled this way before’. Ask what it would mean to keep your eyes on God's presence and not on the water. And ask whether you are crowding in to manage the thing yourself, when you have been told to give God room to go first.

passages.happening:
God speaks to Joshua: “Today I will begin to exalt you in the sight of all Israel, so they may know that I am with you just as I was with Moses” (verse 7). The priests are to carry the ark to the edge of the water and stand in the river (verse 8).

Joshua calls the people to listen. “This is how you will know that the living God is among you and that He will surely drive out before you the Canaanites, Hittites, Hivites, Perizzites, Girgashites, Amorites, and Jebusites” (verse 10). “Behold, the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth will go ahead of you into the Jordan” (verse 11).

He tells them to choose twelve men, one from each tribe (verse 12). And he says what will happen. When the feet of the priests carrying the ark touch the water, the river's ‘flowing waters will be cut off and will stand up in a heap’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
God had promised Joshua in chapter 1 that he would be with him as he was with Moses. Here he says he will show it. Joshua does not make himself great. He stands in front of the people and says in advance what God will do, and then all he can do is wait with everyone else to see if it happens.

Two names for God stand out. ‘The living God’ sets Israel's God against the gods of Canaan, who were worshiped in images of wood, stone and metal. ‘The Lord of all the earth’ makes a claim about who owns the land and its rivers. In the religion of Canaan, power over a river might have been credited to the storm god Baal or to the river itself. Israel is about to be shown whose it is.

The seven peoples in verse 10 are a list that appears often in the books of Moses for those who lived in Canaan. Some are known from records outside the Bible, and some only from the Bible. Seven is a number of completeness in Scripture, and the list stands for everyone in the land.

Joshua says the crossing will be a sign. If God can stop the river, Israel can trust what he has said about the land. The miracle is given to make a frightened people sure of God before they have to face anything else.

The word ‘heap’ is rare in Hebrew. It is the word used in the song Israel sang after the Red Sea, where the waters stood up like a wall. A hearer who knew that song would have caught the echo at once. What God did for the parents he is about to do for the children.

The hard matter of what ‘drive out’ meant for the peoples of the land is taken up in the notes on chapters 6 and 10 and on the book page.
passages.later:
The song at the Red Sea used the same picture: “At the blast of Your nostrils the waters piled up; like a wall the currents stood firm” (Exodus 15:8).

A psalm joins the two crossings in one line and asks the waters why they ran: “Why was it, O sea, that you fled, O Jordan, that you turned back” (Psalm 114:5). It gives the answer: “Tremble, O earth, at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob” (Psalm 114:7).
passages.asks: Joshua told the people what God would do before God did it, and then had to wait and see. Ask whether there is something God has said that you are afraid to count on in front of other people. And think about the two names. Ask what in your life you treat as if it belonged to some other power, and what it would mean to call God the Lord of that too.

passages.happening:
The people break camp. The priests go ahead of them with the ark (verse 14).

The writer stops to remind the reader of the season: “Now the Jordan overflows its banks throughout the harvest season” (verse 15). Then it happens. As soon as the priests reach the river and their feet touch the edge of the water, ‘the flowing water stood still’ (verse 16). It backs up a long way upstream, at a town called Adam. Downstream, the water running toward the Salt Sea is cut off. “So the people crossed over opposite Jericho” (verse 16).

The chapter ends with a still picture. “The priests carrying the ark of the covenant of the LORD stood firm on dry ground in the middle of the Jordan, while all Israel crossed over the dry ground, until the entire nation had crossed the Jordan” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The Jordan is not a wide river. For most of the year it could be forded at known places. In spring it was another thing. Melting snow from Mount Hermon in the far north and the winter rains filled it until it spread over its flood plain. The writer mentions the harvest so that the reader knows the river was at its worst.

The water does not stop while the priests are standing on the bank. It stops when their feet are wet. They had to step into a river in flood on the strength of what Joshua had said.

Adam is usually identified with a site upstream from Jericho, near the place where the Jabbok River joins the Jordan. The Salt Sea is the Dead Sea, into which the Jordan runs.

The words ‘dry ground’ are chosen with care. They are the words used for the crossing of the Red Sea. The book wants its readers to see one event in the other. The generation that came out of Egypt had walked through the sea. Their children, who had only heard about it, now walk through the river.

The picture at the end is worth holding. A nation files past, and in the middle of the riverbed the priests stand still with the ark on their shoulders. The sign of God's presence stays in the place of danger until the last person is across.
passages.later:
Elijah and Elisha later crossed the same river in the same way: Elijah struck the water with his cloak, and it ‘parted to the right and to the left, so that the two of them crossed over on dry ground’ (2 Kings 2:8).

It was to this river that Jesus came at the start of his work: “At that time Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to be baptized by John” (Matthew 3:13). The Gospels do not say that this was meant as an echo of Joshua, and scholars debate it. Christian hymns have often used the crossing of the Jordan as a picture of death and of entering God's final rest. That belongs to later devotion and not to the chapter itself.
passages.hard:
Did the Jordan really stop flowing? How have readers understood it?

Readers have taken the account in three main ways.

Many understand it as a direct act of God beyond any natural cause. The river stopped at the moment the priests stepped in, as the text says.

Others point to the high clay banks near the site usually identified as Adam. Landslides there are reported to have blocked the Jordan for hours on several occasions, including during an earthquake in 1927. On this view God may have used such an event, and the miracle lies in its timing: it came at the hour God had announced, when the ark reached the water.

Critical scholars often read the account as a retelling shaped to mirror the exodus, perhaps connected with later worship at Gilgal, and they are less concerned to work out what happened physically.

These notes do not choose among them. The text does not explain how the water stopped. It says who stopped it and why. The living God, the Lord of all the earth, opened a way into the land as he had opened the sea.
passages.asks: The water did not stop until the priests' feet were in it. Ask where you are waiting on the bank for God to act first, when what he has asked for is the first step. And think of the ark standing in the riverbed until everyone had crossed. Ask who is still in the middle of something hard, and whether you could stand there with them until they are through.
